| TCP sequence number | 32 bits |

steps.body: P → 16 = IV, Q → 48 = I, R → 8 = II, S → 32 = III. So the mapping is **P-IV, Q-I, R-II, S-III**, which is option C.

cse-2018-cs-14.approach: In slow start every ACK adds 1 MSS to cwnd. A window of w segments gets w ACKs per RTT, so cwnd goes from w to 2w each RTT: exponential growth.

steps.body: Each new ACK does $\text{cwnd} \leftarrow \text{cwnd} + 1\,\text{MSS}$. So (i) (adds 2 MSS) is false and (ii) (doubles per ACK) is false.

steps.title: Per RTT
steps.body: With $\text{cwnd} = w$ MSS, one RTT returns $w$ ACKs, so $w \to w + w = 2w$. cwnd **doubles every RTT**: (iv) is true. Growth of 1 MSS per RTT, statement (iii), is congestion avoidance, not slow start.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Only (iv) is true, which is option C.

cse-2018-cs-15.approach: A trial ends the game unless it is a tie. Winning on the 3rd trial means two ties and then a non-tie, a geometric probability.

steps.title: Tie probability
steps.body: A tie needs both dice to show the same face: $P(\text{tie}) = \frac{6}{36} = \frac{1}{6}$, so $P(\text{no tie}) = \frac{5}{6}$.

steps.title: Win on trial 3
steps.body: $$P = \left(\tfrac{1}{6}\right)^2 \cdot \tfrac{5}{6} = \frac{1}{36}\cdot\frac{5}{6} = \frac{5}{216} = 0.023148\ldots$$

steps.title: Round
steps.body: To 3 decimal places: **0.023**.

pitfalls: Using $\frac{1}{2}$ for the non-tie factor: "one of them wins" covers both P and Q winning, so it is the whole $\frac{5}{6}$.
cse-2018-cs-15.verification: $5/216 = 0.0231$; summing over all trials, $\sum_k (1/6)^{k-1}(5/6) = 1$ as expected.

cse-2018-cs-16.approach: Substitute $t = x^2$: the integrand is exactly half the derivative of $\sin(x^2)$.

steps.title: Antiderivative
steps.body:
With $t = x^2$, $dt = 2x\,dx$:
$$\int x\cos(x^2)\,dx = \tfrac{1}{2}\sin(x^2) + C$$

Forgetting the factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$, which gives 0.578.
cse-2018-cs-16.verification: With exact $\pi$: $(\pi/4)^2 = 0.61685$, $\tfrac{1}{2}\sin(0.61685) = 0.2893$, so it still rounds to 0.289.

cse-2018-cs-17.approach: A rank-one matrix $uv^T$ has eigenvalues $v^Tu$ (eigenvector $u$) and 0, so the largest eigenvalue is $v^Tu$.

steps.title: Form A
steps.body: $$A = uv^T = \begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\2 & 2\end{pmatrix}$$

steps.title: Eigenvalues
steps.body: $\det A = 1\cdot2 - 1\cdot2 = 0$, so one eigenvalue is $0$. The trace is $1 + 2 = 3$, so the other is $3 - 0 = 3$. Check: $Au = u(v^Tu) = u\cdot(1+2) = 3u$.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The largest eigenvalue is **3**.

cse-2018-cs-17.shortcut: For $uv^T$ the only non-zero eigenvalue is $v^Tu = 1\cdot1 + 1\cdot2 = 3$.
pitfalls: Computing $u^Tu = 5$ or $v^Tv = 2$ instead of $v^Tu$.

cse-2018-cs-18.approach: Find a triangle to get the lower bound 3, then give an explicit proper 3-colouring to get the upper bound.
cse-2018-cs-18.given: Edges: a–b, a–c, a–e, b–c, b–d, b–f, c–d, c–e, d–f, e–f (6 vertices, 10 edges).

steps.title: Lower bound
steps.body: a, b, c are pairwise adjacent (a–b, a–c, b–c), so they form a triangle and need 3 colours: $\chi \ge 3$.

steps.title: Colour the rest
steps.body:
Use colours 1, 2, 3 with a = 1, b = 2, c = 3.
- e is adjacent to a (1), c (3), f, so e = 2.
- d is adjacent to c (3), b (2), f, so d = 1.
- f is adjacent to b (2), d (1), e (2), so f = 3.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Every edge joins different colours: a–b (1,2), a–c (1,3), a–e (1,2), b–c (2,3), b–d (2,1), b–f (2,3), c–d (3,1), c–e (3,2), d–f (1,3), e–f (2,3). So $\chi \le 3$ and the chromatic number is **3**.

pitfalls: Assuming a 4th colour is needed because of the many edges: the colouring above shows 3 colours are enough.
cse-2018-cs-18.verification: All 10 edges were checked one by one for different colours.

cse-2018-cs-19.approach: By Lagrange the order of a subgroup divides 84. A proper subgroup cannot be all of G, so its order is at most the largest proper divisor, 42. A subgroup of order 42 can exist (index 2, e.g. in the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_{84}$).

steps.title: Achievable
steps.body: In $\mathbb{Z}_{84}$ the subgroup $\langle 2 \rangle = \{0, 2, 4, \ldots, 82\}$ has $84/2 = 42$ elements. So the largest possible proper subgroup size is **42**.

pitfalls: Answering 83: a subgroup order must divide the group order.
Thinking every group of order 84 has a subgroup of order 42. The question asks for the largest *possible* size, which $\mathbb{Z}_{84}$ reaches.

cse-2018-cs-20.approach: Rebuild the tree: the last postorder element is the root, and its position in the inorder sequence splits the left and right subtrees. Repeat, then measure the longest root-to-leaf path in edges.

steps.title: Root 1
steps.body: The last postorder element is **1**. In inorder, left of 1 is {8, 6, 9, 4, 7, 2, 5} and right is {3}.

steps.title: Left subtree root 2
steps.body: The left part in postorder is 8, 9, 6, 7, 4, 5, **2**, so its root is 2. Inorder 8, 6, 9, 4, 7 | 2 | 5: left = {8, 6, 9, 4, 7}, right = {5}.

steps.title: Roots 4 and 6
steps.body: Postorder 8, 9, 6, 7, **4**, so the root is 4. Inorder 8, 6, 9 | 4 | 7: left {8, 6, 9}, right {7}. Postorder 8, 9, **6**, so the root is 6, with left child 8 and right child 9.

steps.title: Height
steps.body: The longest path is $1 \to 2 \to 4 \to 6 \to 8$ (or ending at 9), which has **4 edges**. So the height is **4**.

pitfalls: Counting nodes on the path (5) instead of edges (4); the question defines height as path length.
cse-2018-cs-20.verification: The postorder of the rebuilt tree is 8, 9, 6, 7, 4, 5, 2, 3, 1 and its inorder is 8, 6, 9, 4, 7, 2, 5, 1, 3. Both match the question.

cse-2018-cs-22.approach: The two D flip-flops form a 2-bit shift register. With state $(Q_1Q_2)$ the next state is $(\text{in}, Q_1)$. A self-loop needs $\text{in} = Q_1$ and $Q_1 = Q_2$.

steps.body: $Q_1^+ = \text{in}$, $Q_2^+ = Q_1$. So $(Q_1Q_2) \xrightarrow{\text{in}} (\text{in}\,Q_1)$.

steps.body: Next = current needs $\text{in}\,Q_1 = Q_1Q_2$, so $Q_1 = Q_2$ (and $\text{in} = Q_1$). Only states **00** (in = 0) and **11** (in = 1) qualify. The answer is **2**.

cse-2018-cs-23.approach: All chips are refreshed in parallel. One refresh period needs (rows × time per row-refresh). That fraction of 2 ms is lost; the remainder is available.
cse-2018-cs-23.given:
| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Memory | 1 GB, 32-bit wide |
| Chip | 256M × 4 bit |
| Rows per chip | $2^{14}$ |
| One refresh | 50 ns |
| Refresh period | 2 ms |

steps.title: Chip layout
steps.body: Chip capacity $= 256\text{M} \times 4 \text{ bit} = 128$ MB, so there are $1\text{ GB}/128\text{ MB} = 8$ chips. A 32-bit word needs $32/4 = 8$ chips side by side, so it is one bank and all 8 chips refresh simultaneously.

steps.title: Refresh time per period
steps.body: Each row is refreshed once per period: $2^{14} \times 50\text{ ns} = 16384 \times 50 = 819200\text{ ns} = 0.8192$ ms.

pitfalls: Multiplying the refresh time by the 8 chips: they are refreshed in parallel.
Answering 41 (the refresh share) instead of the available share.

cse-2018-cs-24.approach: Worst case: every process holds $K-1$ instances and waits for one more. Deadlock is impossible if one spare instance still remains, i.e. $n(K-1) + 1 \le R$.

steps.title: Condition
steps.body: With $n = 3$ processes and $R = 4$ instances, deadlock is always avoided iff $3(K - 1) + 1 \le 4$, i.e. $3(K-1) \le 3$, i.e. $K \le 2$.

steps.title: Check both sides
steps.body:
- $K = 2$: at worst each holds 1 ($3$ total) and the 4th instance lets one process finish and release.
- $K = 3$: the allocation (2, 1, 1) uses all 4 instances, and each process still needs more (1, 2 and 2 instances). Nobody can proceed, so this is a deadlock.

The largest safe $K$ is **2**.

pitfalls: Using $nK \le R$ (giving $K = 1$): this is too strict, since a process only needs one extra instance to finish.
cse-2018-cs-24.verification: For K = 3 the allocation (2, 1, 1) uses all 4 instances, and every process still needs at least 1 more, so it deadlocks.

cse-2018-cs-25.approach: TCP sequence numbers count bytes in a 32-bit space. A number repeats after $2^{32}$ bytes have been sent; at full line rate that takes $2^{32}\times 8 / 10^9$ seconds.

steps.title: Sequence space
steps.body: 32-bit field, so $2^{32} = 4294967296$ distinct byte numbers before 1234 comes back.

steps.title: Time
steps.body:
$$T = \frac{2^{32}\times 8\text{ bits}}{10^9\text{ bits/s}} = \frac{34359738368}{10^9} = 34.36\text{ s}$$
Rounded: **34** seconds.

pitfalls: Forgetting that sequence numbers count bytes, not bits (that gives 4.29 s).
The starting value 1234 does not matter; only the size of the space does.

cse-2018-cs-26.approach: P is 2×2 (eigenvectors are 2-vectors). Two distinct eigenvalues would give two independent eigenvectors, so the eigenvalue must be repeated and its eigenspace is 1-dimensional. That makes P defective, so it is not diagonalizable. Nothing forces the eigenvalue to be 0.

steps.title: II is true
steps.body: If $P$ had distinct eigenvalues $\lambda_1 \ne \lambda_2$, their eigenvectors would be independent, giving a direction other than $(1,4)^T$. So $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2$: a repeated eigenvalue.

steps.title: III is true
steps.body: Algebraic multiplicity 2, but geometric multiplicity 1 (only multiples of $(1,4)^T$). There are not enough independent eigenvectors to form a basis, so P cannot be diagonalized.

steps.title: I is not forced
steps.body: Counter-example: $P = \begin{pmatrix}5 & -1\\ 16 & -3\end{pmatrix}$ has trace 2 and $\det P = -15 + 16 = 1$. So $\lambda = 1$ is repeated, and $P - I = \begin{pmatrix}4 & -1\\ 16 & -4\end{pmatrix}$ has null space spanned by $(1,4)^T$. This P fits the question and is invertible. Only II and III are necessarily true: option D.

III is also necessarily true (a defective matrix), so "only II" is incomplete.
I is not necessarily true.
Correct: the eigenvalue is repeated and the eigenspace is deficient, so P is not diagonalizable.

cse-2018-cs-27.approach: Check each set: rationals are countable, a function from {0,1} to N is just an ordered pair in N×N, finite subsets of N are a countable union of countable sets, and functions N → {0,1} are infinite binary sequences, which are uncountable (Cantor diagonal).

steps.body:
**P**: $\mathbb{Q}$ maps injectively into $\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{N}$, so it is countable.
**Q**: $f:\{0,1\}\to\mathbb{N}$ is determined by $(f(0), f(1)) \in \mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, so it is countable.

steps.title: Set R
steps.body: $f:\mathbb{N}\to\{0,1\}$ is an infinite 0/1 sequence, i.e. the characteristic function of a subset of $\mathbb{N}$. So $|R| = |2^{\mathbb{N}}| = 2^{\aleph_0}$, which is uncountable by Cantor's diagonal argument.

steps.title: Set S
steps.body: Finite subsets of size $k$ form a countable set (a subset of $\mathbb{N}^k$). The union over $k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$ is a countable union of countable sets, so S is countable. (Equivalently, map $\{a_1,\ldots,a_k\}$ to $\sum 2^{a_i}$, a bijection with $\mathbb{N}$.) Countable: P, Q, S, which is option D.

cse-2018-cs-28.approach: For a ∃*∀* (Bernays–Schönfinkel) sentence without function symbols, keep only the three elements chosen as witnesses for s, t, u. The universal part still holds on this substructure, so there is a model with at most 3 elements.

steps.title: Take witnesses
steps.body: In the 7-element model M pick $a, b, c$ with $M \models \forall v\forall w\forall x\forall y\,\psi(a,b,c,v,w,x,y)$.

steps.title: Restrict
steps.body: Let $M'$ be M restricted to $\{a,b,c\}$ (at most 3 elements). With no function symbols this is a valid substructure. ψ is quantifier-free, so its truth for any assignment from $\{a,b,c\}$ is the same in $M'$ and M. The universal quantifiers now range over fewer elements, so they still hold. Hence $M' \models \varphi$ with size ≤ 3: option A.

steps.title: Other options
steps.body: B contradicts the model just built. For C and D, take $\psi \equiv (s = s)$ (always true): then φ has models of every size, including 7 and sizes larger than 7, so neither C nor D is necessarily true.

Not necessary: e.g. if ψ is a tautology, φ has models of every size, including more than 7.
Not necessary: the 3-element substructure is already a smaller model.

cse-2018-cs-30.approach: In an undirected DFS every non-tree edge joins an ancestor and a descendant, so I holds. In BFS non-tree edges join vertices whose depths differ by at most 1, and they can have equal depth (e.g. in a triangle), so II fails.

steps.title: Statement I
steps.body: Suppose edge $(u,v)$ and DFS discovers u first. While u is on the stack, v is still unvisited and adjacent, so DFS visits v before u finishes. Then v is a descendant of u. So every edge is a tree edge or a back edge: **no cross edges**. I is true.

steps.title: Statement II
steps.body: Counter-example: triangle $x, y, z$ with BFS from x. Then y and z are at depth 1, and edge $(y,z)$ has $|1 - 1| = 0 \ne 1$. BFS guarantees only $|i - j| \le 1$. II is false.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: I only, which is option A.

cse-2018-cs-34.approach: Split the P-bit byte address into tag | set index | block offset. Offset = bits to address a byte inside a $2^{M}$-word block of $2^{W}$-byte words; sets = cache size / (block size × K).

steps.body:
Block size $= 2^M \cdot 2^W = 2^{M+W}$ bytes, so the offset is $M + W$ bits.
Number of blocks $= 2^N / 2^{M+W} = 2^{N-M-W}$; sets $= 2^{N-M-W}/K$, so the index is $N - M - W - \log_2 K$ bits.

steps.title: Tag
steps.body: $$\text{tag} = P - (N - M - W - \log_2 K) - (M + W) = P - N + \log_2 K$$ This is option B.

optionAnalysis.reason: Sign error: more ways means fewer sets, so the tag gets longer by $\log_2 K$, not shorter.
Correct.
